title: Missing Number Detective
description: One of the three numbers is hidden, or one digit is, and the two that are left are enough to find it.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Find the number, or the single digit, that somebody has hidden in a subtraction, using only the two that are still showing.
writeup.look: A column mat with one row blank or a scatter of stars across it, a mode rail above and a build bay waiting underneath.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Missing Number Detective' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many of the three rows are filled against how many the puzzle has, two numbers side by side in ink, and under them the name of whatever is blank, written in words: the number on top, the number taken away, or a single digit. On the third phase it carries how many stars are still covered. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The mode rail runs along the top of the working area, three keys 236 by 48 at 64,202, at 316,202 and at 568,202, reading the number on top, the number taken away and single digits, with the chosen one standing proud of the other two. The name it first gate is 330 by 48 at 820,202, three small rows inside it naming the three things that can be blank, and until one is picked nothing on the mat will move at all; a wrong pick names none of the others and the gate simply asks again. The column mat is 700 by 242 at 64,266: a trade strip 34 tall across its top, where a lending digit is struck through once with its new and smaller value written small above it and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column it went to; a heading row 36 tall of six ruled cells reading L, TTh, Th, H, T and O; the number on top 56 tall in deep blue; the number taken away 56 tall in amber with a minus drawn to the left of its row; a rule 4 tall; and the answer row 56 tall in green under the rule. A blank row keeps its cells ruled and empty rather than closing up, so the mat never stops looking like a subtraction. The build bay is 700 by 150 at 64,530 and opens only in the first two modes: it stacks the two rows that are showing, draws a plus when the blank is the number on top and a minus when the blank is the number taken away, works its own columns with a trade strip of its own above them, and lifts its result up into the empty row rather than printing it twice. Star cards are 56 by 56 plain ink cards with a star drawn on each, and they sit directly over single digits across all three rows. The reasoning strip is 330 by 242 at 820,266 and opens when a column is tapped: it stands that column's known digits one under the other, leaves the covered cell open, draws any ten coming into it from the column on its right, and prints the column's name at its head. A column tapped before the column on its right has been settled is refused, and the column that has to come first lights instead. Settling a column whose two lower digits pass nine drops a ten into the column on its left by itself, small and vermilion above the heading, because a subtraction read upwards is an addition and an addition carries leftwards; the same trade read downwards is that left hand column lending a ten and being left one less, and the strip prints both readings of it at once. The check it back control is 180 by 44 at 64,686, and it works the finished subtraction downwards in its own columns and sets the answer it reaches beside the answer that was printed there all along. On the fourth phase the single mat is replaced by three small mats 354 by 242 at 64,266, at 430,266 and at 796,266, each with a different row blank and its own gate closed in front of it. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number or a single digit has to be written, with a thirteenth key that writes a run of zeros so a round number can be finished in one press. On the third phase a strip of six place words, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands and lakhs, sits under the keys, because the column being settled is named before a digit is typed into it. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of a column is vermilion and is always drawn small above the column it arrives in, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, and a trade is told by the strike through the lending digit and by the smaller value written above it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the hardest puzzle the child finished, with what they found still lit and the downward check standing beside it.

phases.win: the total rises into the blank row and the subtraction reads straight through
phases.does: drops the two showing numbers into the build bay and adds them
phases.goal: the difference and the subtrahend rebuild the number on top
phases.says: The top row is empty. Add the two you can see and see where they land.
phases.check: The number taken away was 5,286 and the answer was 4,694. What was on top, and how would you show me you are right?
phases.feels: the puzzle says take away and the thing that solves it turns out to be adding
phases.hands: Write the number taken away and the answer on two paper slips, lay them one under the other with their right ends level, add them on squared paper, and then write the whole subtraction out with that total on top and work it downwards.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the three rows on your mat is empty? Second rung, the phase's: do the two you can see add up to it, or take away from it? Third rung: the mat is cut to a two digit pair and the bay stacks them with a plus already drawn, so the move is seen before the numbers get long. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: every working in the chapter so far has ended in a taking away, so two numbers with a blank standing above them look like a subtraction waiting to be done.
wrong.move: takes the smaller of the two showing numbers off the greater one, because the puzzle is a subtraction.
wrong.screen: the build bay fills with the two showing numbers and works them both ways at once in its two halves: 4,694 and 5,286 added give 9,980, and the greater less the smaller gives 592. Each answer is lifted into the blank row in turn and the whole subtraction is read downwards from it, and only the number built by adding leaves 5,286 taken away with 4,694 standing under the rule. Nothing is cleared and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a written line begins at its left hand end, and beginning together is what lining up looks like.
wrong.move: lines a three digit number taken away under a four digit answer by their left ends in the build bay.
wrong.screen: the heading over every digit of the shorter card is named under it as the card slides, and the card carries on sliding right until its last digit stands in the ones column, leaving its left hand column ruled and empty rather than closing the gap up. The rule and the total row stay empty the whole time it moves, so nothing is added until the places agree; with 986 under 4,694 by their right ends the total is 5,680, and 5,680 less 986 leaves 4,694 standing under the rule.

phases.screen: the mat with the upper row blank and both other rows showing
phases.soWhat: When the number on top is missing, the answer and the number taken away add back to it, so the check I already had is also the tool that finds it.
phases.concept: A missing greater number is built by adding

phases.win: the answer drops into the middle row and adding all three back agrees
phases.does: sets out the number on top less the difference and works it
phases.goal: the difference comes off the number on top to give the subtrahend
phases.says: This time the middle row is empty. Is adding still the move?
phases.check: The number on top was 9,625 and the answer was 3,289. What was taken away, and what should adding your two lower rows give you back?
phases.feels: the same mat, the same two numbers showing, and the move flips over
phases.hands: Write the number on top and the answer on squared paper one under the other, take the second off the first, then write all three out as a subtraction and add the lower two to watch the top one come back.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which row is empty this time? Second rung, the phase's: is that row above the rule or under it? Third rung: the bay is cut to the number on top and the answer with a minus already drawn between them, so only the working is left to do. The pad stays open and nothing already written is taken away.

wrong.why: the move that worked a moment ago is the move nearest to hand, and the two puzzles look alike on the mat.
wrong.move: adds the two showing numbers, because adding is what the last phase wanted.
wrong.screen: the bay builds both and leaves them side by side. Adding 9,625 and 3,289 gives 12,914, which will not go into a middle row under a number smaller than itself, and the mat is shown with no room for it; taking away gives 6,336, and putting 6,336 into the middle row leaves 3,289 standing under the rule where it was printed. Neither working is crossed out.

wrong.why: the two lower rows carry numbers of much the same size, and the blank does not say which of them belongs where.
wrong.move: puts the answer into the middle row and the number taken away into the answer row, swapping the two lower rows over.
wrong.screen: the mat reads itself back with its row names printed down the left margin and the subtraction worked downwards, each row named aloud as it is used. With 3,289 in the middle the answer comes to 6,336, and with 6,336 in the middle the answer comes to 3,289, so both fill the mat and only one of them answers the question that was asked. The question card stays lit above the mat the whole time.

phases.screen: the mat with the middle row blank and the top and answer rows showing
phases.soWhat: When the number taken away is missing, the answer comes off the number on top, and what is left is the number that was taken away.
phases.concept: A missing smaller number is found by taking away

phases.win: the star lifts, the column reads both ways and any ten appears on its left
phases.does: starts at the ones, rebuilds the column upwards and types the digit in
phases.goal: a covered digit is read out of its own column, starting at the ones
phases.says: Read it upwards. The answer and the number taken away add back to the top.
phases.check: A puzzle reads 8*51 - 26*4 = 5677, with one star on the top row and one in the number taken away. Which column do you settle first, and what are the two hidden digits?
phases.feels: an answer that adds back perfectly turns out not to fit, and the cells printed on the page are the thing that says so
phases.hands: Write a subtraction out in full on squared paper and check it by addition, then cover two single digits with torn paper, hand it to somebody else, and afterwards ask them which column they settled first.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column on your mat has only one thing missing in it? Second rung, the phase's: what do the answer's digit and the number taken away's digit come to when you add them inside that column? Third rung: the mat is cut to the ones column alone with its two known digits lit and the cell above them open, so one column is settled before any other is offered. Nothing lifted is ever put back.

wrong.why: a covered digit in the middle looks no harder than one at the end, and there is nothing printed on the page saying where to begin.
wrong.move: tackles a starred column in the middle of the number before the columns on its right have been settled.
wrong.screen: the column that was tapped dims and the ones column lights instead, with the column lock naming it aloud. On 7,242 less 3,417 the ones are settled first, the answer's five and the number taken away's seven making twelve, so the digit on top is two and a ten rides up into the tens on its left. Only then will the tens column open, and the middle column the child reached for is still sitting there untouched. The whole puzzle rebuilds to 7,242 less 3,417, which leaves 3,825, and its ones and its hundreds are the two columns that had to fetch a ten.

wrong.why: the check by addition is the check this chapter has taught, and an answer that passes it feels finished.
wrong.move: hands in an answer that adds back perfectly and does not fit the cells the page prints.
wrong.screen: the two candidates are stood one above the other with the printed row of cells drawn over each of them. On the puzzle whose cells read eight, blank, seven, two, blank on top and five, six, six, blank, seven underneath, 87,724 less 27,117 comes to 60,607 and adds back exactly, and the cell drawn over its first digit is printed as a five while a six is standing in it. The other candidate, 83,724 less 27,117, comes to 56,607, and every one of its digits drops into a cell that is either blank or already says that digit. Neither working is crossed out and the cells stay drawn over both.

phases.screen: a subtraction with stars in two rows and every column tappable
phases.soWhat: A starred sum is a pattern as well as a subtraction, so settle the columns from the ones and check that every digit you write lands in a cell that will hold it.
phases.concept: A missing digit is found by rebuilding its column

phases.win: each gate opens on a correct naming and each puzzle takes a different move
phases.does: names the blank on each one, then works the move that blank needs
phases.goal: naming the blank decides which of the three moves is needed
phases.says: Before you work anything, say which of the three is hiding.
phases.check: Point at the blank in this puzzle and tell me its name before you work anything. Now what are you going to do, and why that?
phases.feels: the puzzles stop being three kinds of thing and turn into one question asked about three different rows
phases.hands: Write three puzzles out on one sheet with a different thing blank in each, and have the child write add, take away or settle the columns beside each one before any working is begun.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which row is the blank standing in? Second rung, the phase's: is that row above the rule or under it? Third rung: the three mats are cut to one at a time with the gate open in front of it, so the blank is named before the bay will draw any sign at all. Nothing named wrongly is ever marked, and the gate simply asks again.

wrong.why: three puzzles set out side by side look like three helpings of one question, and the move that worked on the first is the move nearest to hand.
wrong.move: works the first puzzle correctly and then uses that same move on the next two without looking at what is blank in them.
wrong.screen: the three mats lift their blank rows together and each one is named in the margin beside it: the number on top on the first, the number taken away on the second, a single digit on the third. The bay under each mat then draws the sign that mat needs, a plus under the first, a minus under the second and a column strip under the third, so all three moves stand on the stage at the same time. Nothing already worked is cleared.

wrong.why: naming has been a thing said out loud rather than a thing used, so it goes past without changing what the hands do.
wrong.move: names the blank correctly and then works the other move anyway, because two numbers showing are in the habit of being added.
wrong.screen: the naming the child gave is printed on a card above the bay and stays there while the working runs, and the sign in the bay is drawn from that card rather than chosen: a blank on top draws a plus, a blank in the middle draws a minus, and a blank under the rule draws a minus too, because that is an ordinary subtraction. With 888 and 384 showing and the row under the rule blank, the bay draws a minus and the seat gap comes to 504, which is the question the opening page asked and then left standing. The card and the working are left side by side.

phases.screen: three puzzles side by side with different rows blank and the gate closed
phases.soWhat: Name what is blank first. A blank on top is built by adding, a blank in the middle is found by taking away, and a covered digit is settled column by column from the ones.
phases.concept: Say which number is missing before you start

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the ones column is settled on a puzzle where it passes nine. On 7,242 less 3,417 the answer's five and the number taken away's seven are added inside their own column, the total runs past nine and will not sit in a cell that holds one digit, and the ten it cannot keep rides up out of the column and comes down small and vermilion above the tens on its left. Nothing has been typed into the tens yet and it is already easier than it was, because a column that had two unknowns in it now has one. Then the same trade is redrawn the other way, as the finished subtraction will show it: the tens lending a ten to the ones and being left one less, four written down as three. One trade, two readings, and the star in the ones lifts under a finger. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the column mat stands ruled under its headings with its upper row empty, the number taken away and the answer both printed in their own rows, and the build bay drawn open and empty beneath the mat with a plus already in it. On the second the same mat has its middle row empty instead, and the bay below carries a minus and a rule. On the third the mat is full and starred: single digits are covered across all three rows, the ones column is the only one lit, and the trade strip above the headings is drawn and empty. On the fourth three small mats stand side by side with a different row blank on each and the name it first gate closed in front of all three. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the blank row on the mat, or the rightmost star card, or the closed gate, gives one slow pulse while the voice says that one of the three numbers is hiding. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any subtraction with anything covered, and the build bay, the column lock and the downward check all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on building a missing number on top, finding a missing number taken away, lifting a covered digit, and saying which move a puzzle needs.
voiceLines: One of the three numbers is hiding. Say which one.
The top row is empty. Add the two you can see and see where they land.
This time the middle row is empty. Is adding still the move?
Read it upwards. The answer and the number taken away add back to the top.
Before you work anything, say which of the three is hiding.
Another puzzle. Something else is covered this time.
Free play. Cover a whole number or a single digit, and the build bay stays open.
Name what is blank again, then settle the ones column before any other.
You named what was hiding before you went looking for it, every single time.

observations.why: The answer and the number taken away rebuild the number on top, which is the chapter's own check used the other way about.
observations.soWhat: A missing number on top is found by adding, and the check I already had is the thing that finds it.
observations.observe: The two numbers that were showing added back to exactly the number that had been covered: 4,694 and 5,286 gave 9,980, and taking 5,286 off 9,980 gave 4,694 again.

observations.why: The move is decided by which of the three rows is blank, not by what the puzzle looks like.
observations.soWhat: Naming the blank out loud is the first move, and it is the move that picks the other two.
observations.observe: One puzzle was solved by adding and the next one, which looked the same on the mat, needed taking away: 9,625 with an answer of 3,289 gave 6,336.

observations.why: That page prints the answer row as five, six, six, a blank and seven, and 60,607 puts a six in the cell that is printed as a five.
observations.soWhat: A starred sum is a pattern as well as a subtraction, so a digit has to fit the cell it lands in before it can be right.
observations.observe: An answer of 60,607 added back to 27,117 perfectly and the puzzle still would not take it.

observations.why: The first cell of that answer row is holding a zero, so 6,379 sits in five cells rather than four.
observations.soWhat: Count the cells the page prints before deciding how long an answer is allowed to be.
observations.observe: On one puzzle four of the five columns had to fetch a ten, and the answer row had five cells with only four of them filled.

phases.screen: the mat with the upper row blank and both other rows showing
phases.win: the total rises into the blank row and the subtraction reads straight through
phases.traceback: If the child took one showing number off the other, that working is set under the bay in ink; then the two rows drop into the bay under a plus and are added from the ones, each ten carried left; the total rises into the empty top row and the subtraction is checked downwards.
ladder: Which of the three rows on your mat is empty?
Which row has nothing in it, and which two rows can you still see?
Point to the empty row. Is it the number on top?
Do the two you can see add up to it, or take away from it?
Stack the two you can see in the bay. Add them, starting at the ones.

phases.screen: the mat with the middle row blank and the top and answer rows showing
phases.win: the answer drops into the middle row and adding all three back agrees
phases.traceback: If the child added the two showing, that working is set under the bay in ink; then the number on top and the answer drop into the bay under a minus and are worked from the ones, one ten unbundled at a time, each lending digit struck through in ink with its new value in rose; the result drops into the middle row and the subtraction is checked.
ladder: Which row is empty this time?
Which two rows can you see, and which one is hiding?
Is the hiding number the one on top, or the one taken away?
Is that row above the rule or under it?
Set the answer under the number on top. Take it away, starting at the ones.

phases.screen: a subtraction with stars in two rows and every column tappable
phases.win: the star lifts, the column reads both ways and any ten appears on its left
phases.traceback: The columns are read upwards from the ones: each star lifts, the column's total shows the ten it sends left in vermilion, the ten lands small above the next column, the column is read downwards too, and the whole subtraction is checked.
ladder: Which column on your mat has only one thing missing in it?
Which column is the star in, and is the column to its right settled?
Which two digits can you see in the star's column?
Read that column upwards. The answer's digit and the digit taken away make the top digit.
Start at the ones column and settle it before any other.

phases.screen: three puzzles side by side with different rows blank and the gate closed
phases.win: each gate opens on a correct naming and each puzzle takes a different move
phases.traceback: The three puzzles are named in their margins with the sign each needs: the number on top (+), the number taken away (−) and, on the third, the answer under the rule (−). If the child added the two showing out of habit, that working is set beside the bay in ink; then the bay works the move the current blank needs, lifts the result into its empty row and checks it downwards.
ladder: Which row is the blank standing in?
Which of the three names fits the empty row here?
Where is the empty row: on top, in the middle, or under the rule?
Is that row above the rule or under it?
A blank on top is built by adding. Any other blank is found by taking away.

moves.answer: number on top − number taken away

model.bay: stacks the two rows that show under the sign the blank needs, works its own columns from the ones and lifts the result into the empty row
model.trades: a ten on the move is small and vermilion above the column it reaches; a digit that lent is struck through in ink with its new value small in rose
model.stars: ink cards over single digits; typed digits land on them from the ones leftwards; a column opens only when every column to its right is settled
model.gate: phase 4: the empty row is named (on top, taken away, the answer) before the bay draws any sign

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: If the child took one showing number off the other, that working is set under the bay in ink; then the two rows drop into the bay under a plus and are added from the ones, each ten carried left; the total rises into the empty top row and the subtraction is checked downwards.

Phase 2: If the child added the two showing, that working is set under the bay in ink; then the number on top and the answer drop into the bay under a minus and are worked from the ones, one ten unbundled at a time, each lending digit struck through in ink with its new value in rose; the result drops into the middle row and the subtraction is checked.

Phase 3: The columns are read upwards from the ones: each star lifts, the column's total shows the ten it sends left in vermilion, the ten lands small above the next column, the column is read downwards too, and the whole subtraction is checked.

Phase 4: The three puzzles are named in their margins with the sign each needs: the number on top (+), the number taken away (−) and, on the third, the answer under the rule (−). If the child added the two showing out of habit, that working is set beside the bay in ink; then the bay works the move the current blank needs, lifts the result into its empty row and checks it downwards.

voice.opening: One of the three numbers is hiding. Say which one.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: You named what was hiding before you went looking for it, every single time.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: A missing greater number is built by adding
A missing smaller number is found by taking away
A missing digit is found by rebuilding its column
Say which number is missing before you start

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted, speaking, voice, mascot, summaryRow, played, phase, minuend, null, subtrahend, null, difference, null, covered, length, found, length, columnSettled

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files: correct, wrong (soft), win, and a tick when a piece snaps

voiceLines.en: One of the three numbers is hiding. Say which one.
The top row is empty. Add the two you can see and see where they land.
This time the middle row is empty. Is adding still the move?
Read it upwards. The answer and the number taken away add back to the top.
Before you work anything, say which of the three is hiding.
Another puzzle. Something else is covered this time.
Free play. Cover a whole number or a single digit, and the build bay stays open.
Name what is blank again, then settle the ones column before any other.
You named what was hiding before you went looking for it, every single time.
